passages.title: Checkout downstream errors and bad gateway responses
passages.heading: HTTP 502 from checkout
passages.body: A checkout bad gateway response means a downstream call failed or could not complete. Inspect the ERROR record for its dependency field. Payment dependency and downstream status 503 support a failed payment boundary. Checkout status alone cannot distinguish payment from inventory failure or a network timeout.

passages.title: Checkout downstream errors and bad gateway responses
passages.heading: Follow the failing dependency
passages.body: Use the checkout request ID and incident window to inspect the named dependency's logs. Compare its HTTP status with the caller's downstream error. Successful neighboring requests are counterevidence to a continuous outage. Missing downstream records may mean unavailable telemetry, transport failure, or a mismatched time window.

passages.title: Checkout downstream errors and bad gateway responses
passages.heading: Verification and limits
passages.body: Read-only verification compares both sides of the request with the applicable service map. Do not restart services, change settings, or retry a real payment merely because a runbook suggests a hypothesis. Recovery after an operator action establishes observed recovery, not proof of the original cause.

passages.title: Applicability of versioned operational guidance
passages.heading: Environment and release
passages.body: Choose guidance for the incident environment and release, retaining applicable global guidance. A staging or archived release procedure can describe different dependencies. Similar words do not override applicability metadata.

passages.title: Applicability of versioned operational guidance
passages.heading: Revision reproducibility
passages.body: Preserve the knowledge revision and immutable passage references used by an investigation. Publishing a new index must not rewrite old citations or silently change follow-up retrieval in an ongoing investigation. A failed publication leaves the previous corpus usable.

passages.title: Process liveness versus business availability
passages.heading: A reachable process can reject work
passages.body: A successful health endpoint establishes that the service process responded. It does not establish that payment charge requests or inventory business requests succeeded. Compare business request status and correlated caller logs before claiming recovery or availability.

passages.title: Process liveness versus business availability
passages.heading: Observed recovery
passages.body: A later business request returning HTTP 200 demonstrates recovery for that request at that time. It does not prove service health during an earlier incident or reveal why the earlier request failed. Avoid extending one observation into a continuous availability claim.

passages.title: Cart validation and HTTP client errors
passages.heading: Invalid carts
passages.body: The checkout schema accepts the book item and quantities from one through ten. A missing or invalid field, zero quantity, or quantity eleven is rejected with HTTP 422 before business processing. Extra fields are forbidden. Invalid input is not evidence of a failing dependency.

passages.title: Cart validation and HTTP client errors
passages.heading: Client errors versus dependency failures
passages.body: HTTP 422 describes invalid cart input. HTTP 502 describes checkout failing to complete a downstream call. Compare the response, dependency field, and correlated logs. Do not attribute a rejected cart to payment or inventory without observations of those services.

passages.title: Inventory availability and checkout failures
passages.heading: Inventory is checked before payment
passages.body: Checkout queries inventory availability before payment. If inventory fails, checkout records inventory as the dependency and does not proceed to payment. A missing payment call may be expected control flow. Do not diagnose payment solely because checkout did not finish.

passages.title: Inventory availability and checkout failures
passages.heading: Compare inventory observations
passages.body: Use the same request ID and window to compare inventory and checkout. Inventory 200 with a later payment failure argues against inventory causing that request's checkout error. Unavailable inventory telemetry cannot establish inventory health, even if another source returns no errors.

passages.title: Missing logs and insufficient evidence
passages.heading: Empty results versus unavailable sources
passages.body: A successful query with zero matching records differs from a timeout, unreadable log file, or unavailable service telemetry. Empty results cover only the requested service, time window, and retained data. An unavailable source provides no evidence that requests were healthy.

passages.title: Missing logs and insufficient evidence
passages.heading: Retention and truncated evidence
passages.body: Local logs rotate and queries return a bounded number of records. Truncated responses may omit relevant errors; older coverage after rotation cannot be guaranteed. Preserve truncation and the query window. Do not describe retained records as a complete incident history.

passages.title: Missing logs and insufficient evidence
passages.heading: Abstain when support is missing
passages.body: Separate observed facts from possible explanations. A runbook provides general guidance, not a current incident observation. If no available observation distinguishes competing causes, mark the cause inconclusive and suggest permitted read-only checks. A retrieval score is not a calibrated probability.

passages.title: Dependency timeouts and network reachability
passages.heading: Response failure versus transport failure
passages.body: A downstream request failed record with an HTTP status means an error response was received. A downstream request unavailable record without a status indicates a transport problem such as timeout, name resolution failure, or refused connection. This generic message does not distinguish those causes. Do not claim an unmeasured timeout duration.

passages.title: Dependency timeouts and network reachability
passages.heading: Bounded requests
passages.body: Checkout configures a one-second HTTP client timeout for dependency calls and does not retry transactions automatically. Compare recorded duration, neighboring requests, and downstream logs. The configured timeout does not prove that every unavailable response was a timeout. Timeout categories apply to phases of the HTTP operation rather than guaranteeing a one-second total duration.

passages.title: Dependency timeouts and network reachability
passages.heading: Read-only follow-up
passages.body: Compare dependency health, request errors, and available configuration evidence. A later successful response does not prove connectivity during the incident. Missing network observations should be listed as missing evidence rather than converted into a specific transport diagnosis.

passages.title: Payment unavailable and HTTP 503 investigation
passages.heading: Payment HTTP 503
passages.body: Payment service unavailable records that processing could not complete. Correlate payment HTTP 503 with checkout's payment dependency error using the request ID. Report payment unavailability as an observed symptom. A generic unavailable response does not establish a database, deployment, or upstream-provider diagnosis.

passages.title: Payment unavailable and HTTP 503 investigation
passages.heading: Competing explanations
passages.body: The payment process may be reachable while business processing is unavailable. Successful process health does not refute payment request errors. Consider application rejection, temporary capacity limits, configuration problems, and connectivity only when supported by the applicable architecture and additional observations. This simulation has no external payment gateway or application database.

passages.title: Payment unavailable and HTTP 503 investigation
passages.heading: Check impact and recovery
passages.body: Compare failed and successful payment requests across the incident window. Matching checkout failures establish user-visible impact. If requests later return 200, report recovery at that time. If signals cannot distinguish causes, provide an inconclusive cause and suggested checks instead of unsupported certainty.

passages.title: Deployment timing and causal investigation
passages.heading: Timing is not causation
passages.body: An error beginning near a deployment is a useful lead, not proof of a regression. Compare affected and unaffected services, request IDs, signatures, and observations before and after the change. Determine whether the deployed component is on the failing dependency path.

passages.title: Deployment timing and causal investigation
passages.heading: Missing deployment history
passages.body: This release has no deployment-history tool. If deployment events cannot be observed, state that limitation instead of inventing a timeline. A user's description of a change should be distinguished from independently collected deployment evidence.

passages.title: Deployment timing and causal investigation
passages.heading: Applicability of guidance
passages.body: Use guidance for the correct environment and release. Older architecture may describe dependencies that no longer exist. Cite the document revision and preserve the observation window. Relevant documentation suggests checks but cannot establish that a particular change caused this incident.

passages.title: Request ID correlation across HTTP services
passages.heading: Joining observations
passages.body: Use request_id to join checkout, inventory, and payment logs in the same observation window. Accepted IDs contain exactly 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Invalid supplied IDs are replaced at ingress. Timestamp proximity alone does not establish that two errors belong to the same request.

passages.title: Request ID correlation across HTTP services
passages.heading: Partial correlation
passages.body: A matching request ID supports following a dependency boundary. A missing match can arise from log retention, an incorrect time window, a transport failure, or a request that never reached the downstream service. Preserve missing evidence; do not invent a trace or assume downstream success.

passages.title: Read-only investigation and transaction retry safety
passages.heading: No automatic transaction retries
passages.body: Checkout does not automatically retry inventory or payment transactions. The investigator's tools only read observations and reviewed guidance. Suggested verification steps must not become automatic restarts, configuration changes, repeated charges, or shell execution.

passages.title: Read-only investigation and transaction retry safety
passages.heading: Guidance is not evidence
passages.body: A procedure describes what an operator might verify. It does not establish that its described failure is happening now. Link current observations to each hypothesis, acknowledge contradictory evidence, and leave the underlying cause inconclusive when available signals cannot distinguish alternatives.

passages.title: Shopping service dependencies and boundaries
passages.heading: Request flow
passages.body: Checkout calls inventory availability first, then payment processing. Inventory success does not establish payment success. If inventory fails, checkout stops without calling payment. Use the dependency name as well as the response status to localize the failing boundary.

passages.title: Shopping service dependencies and boundaries
passages.heading: Request correlation
passages.body: Checkout propagates a valid request ID to inventory and payment. Compare records from the same request and incident window. A shared ID links observations but does not identify the underlying cause. Match service, timestamp, dependency, and status before correlating unrelated errors.

passages.title: Shopping service dependencies and boundaries
passages.heading: Supported architecture
passages.body: This release is an HTTP shopping simulation. It has no real payment gateway, order database, customer accounts, or stock reservation. Do not infer database connection exhaustion or external financial failures without an applicable architecture revision and actual observations. Process health is separate from successful business requests.

passages.title: Operational log adapter availability
passages.heading: Adapter failure outcomes
passages.body: source_timeout, source_unreachable, source_http_error, and invalid_source_response mean logs are unavailable. These adapter errors do not prove target application failure or target health. A successful empty query is a different outcome. Preserve the source error, query scope, and truncation status.

passages.title: Operational log adapter availability
passages.heading: Bounded evidence reads
passages.body: The adapter permits a fixed configured source URL, a service allowlist, ordered incident windows no longer than an hour, at most 100 returned records, and a response-size cap. It does not accept arbitrary SQL, shell commands, or user-selected destinations.
